headline: India published a government reference price for GPU time: about Rs 115.85 per GPU hour, and Rs 150 per hour for high-end compute.

headline: Malaysia now requires a strategic trade permit and 30 days' notice to export, tranship or transit US-origin high-performance AI chips.
notes: Effective 2025-07-14. Legal basis: Strategic Trade Act 2010, applied through a Catch-All Control provision placing the items on the Strategic Items List. Requirements: a Strategic Trade Permit before export, plus a minimum 30-day advance notification before exporting, transhipping or transiting. MITI said violators face strict legal action under the STA 2010 or related laws. The directive does not enumerate specific ECCNs or chip models in this source. PRACTICAL EFFECT: a Malaysian re-export of US-origin AI chips now needs both a US licence (see the worldwide 3A090.a requirement) and a Malaysian permit. Primary MITI pages could not be reached from this network; this record rests on a single trade-press account and should be upgraded to T1 against MITI's own directive before being relied on.

headline: The US published the AI Diffusion rule, sorting the world into a licence-free top tier, a capped middle and a denied tier.
notes: Federal Register citation 90 FR 4544, document 2025-00636, published 2025-01-15, effective 2025-01-13, general compliance date 2025-05-15 with some provisions to 2026-01-15. UNIT IS TOTAL PROCESSING PERFORMANCE (TPP), a cumulative installed-base cap, not an annual figure. Top tier (Supplement No. 5 to Part 740, paragraph (a)) included, from Asia-Pacific: Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Republic of Korea and Taiwan. India, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines were NOT in the top tier and fell under the per-country TPP cap.
quantity_raw: per-country allocation of 790,000,000 TPP for the period from 2025 to 2027

headline: The US Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the AI Diffusion rule and would replace it, but as of September 2026 the rule text is still in the regulations.
notes: BIS announced on 2025-05-13 that it had instructed enforcement officials not to enforce the AI Diffusion Rule, and said it 'plans to publish a regulation formalizing the rescission and will issue a replacement rule in the future'. CRITICAL AND EASILY MISSED: a Federal Register search of all BIS documents from 2025-05-01 to 2026-09-02 returns no rule formalising that rescission, and the eCFR text current to 2026-08-31 still contains Supplement No. 5 to Part 740 (Artificial Intelligence Authorization Countries), License Exception AIA at 15 CFR 740.27, and the 790,000,000 TPP per-country allocations at 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(B). So the framework remains codified law while being formally unenforced. Anyone relying on either state alone will get the legality of an APAC deal wrong. Text verified against the eCFR snapshot for 2026-08-31 retrieved through the eCFR versioner API (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-31/title-15.xml?part=740 and ...?part=742). The canonical eCFR HTML section URLs are cited alongside; they returned a bot-block redirect from this network, not a 404.

headline: A US export licence is required worldwide for top-end datacentre AI chips, and the only licence-free route covers Australia, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and New Zealand - not India, Singapore or the rest of Southeast Asia.
notes: STATE OF THE RULES as of the eCFR text current to 2026-08-31 - this is the record that decides whether an APAC match is legal. (1) 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A): a licence is required to export, reexport or transfer ECCN 3A090.a, 4A090.a and the corresponding .z entries 'to or within any destination worldwide'. (2) License Exception ACA (15 CFR 740.8) authorises such items worldwide EXCEPT Macau/Country Group D:5 - but expressly EXCLUDES 'items designed or marketed for use in a datacenter and meeting the parameters of 3A090.a', so it does not help for datacentre GPUs. (3) License Exception AIA (15 CFR 740.27) does cover datacentre 3A090.a, but only to entities located in Supplement No. 5(a) destinations, which in Asia-Pacific are Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Republic of Korea and Taiwan, and only if the entity is not headquartered outside that list. (4) Consequence: for INDIA, SINGAPORE, MALAYSIA, INDONESIA, THAILAND, VIETNAM and the PHILIPPINES there is a licence requirement for datacentre-class 3A090.a with NO available licence exception. (5) Licence review policy, 742.6(b)(10)(iii): presumption of approval for Supplement 5(a) countries; for all other destinations presumption of approval only up to the 790,000,000 TPP per-country allocation for 2025-2027, and a POLICY OF DENIAL once that allocation is exhausted. BIS was to publish progress at bis.gov/advanced-compute-resources, but that page reads only 'Coming soon!' as of 2026-09-02, so no country's remaining headroom is public. (6) 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(B): lower-tier 3A090.b needs a licence to the UAE and to Country Groups D:1/D:4/D:5 excluding A:5/A:6 - in Asia-Pacific that catches China, Macau, North Korea and VIETNAM. Text verified against the eCFR snapshot for 2026-08-31 retrieved through the eCFR versioner API (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-31/title-15.xml?part=740 and ...?part=742). The canonical eCFR HTML section URLs are cited alongside; they returned a bot-block redirect from this network, not a 404.
quantity_raw: worldwide licence requirement for ECCN 3A090.a and 4A090.a and corresponding .z items

headline: Where each Asia-Pacific country sits in the US export control country groups as of August 2026.
notes: From Supplement No. 1 to Part 740, eCFR text current to 2026-08-31. GROUP A:5 (closest tier): Australia, India, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, and the United Arab Emirates (added July 2026). GROUP A:6: Singapore, Taiwan. NEITHER A NOR D - i.e. only Country Group B: Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Philippines. GROUP D:1 (national security): China, North Korea, Macau, VIETNAM. GROUP D:3 (chemical and biological): China, North Korea, Macau, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan, Vietnam. GROUP D:4 (missile technology): China, North Korea, Macau, Saudi Arabia. GROUP D:5 (US arms embargoed): China, North Korea. GROUP E:1: North Korea. IMPORTANT NUANCE: A:5/A:6 membership is NOT the same as AI chip eligibility. India is A:5 but is absent from Supplement No. 5, so it gets no AI licence exception; Taiwan is only A:6 but IS in Supplement No. 5, so it does. Saudi Arabia sits in D:3 and D:4 but not D:1 or D:5. Separately, 742.6(b)(8) gives India a general policy of approval for licence applications for civil or military end uses, which does not displace the advanced-computing rules in 742.6(a)(6). Text verified against the eCFR snapshot for 2026-08-31 retrieved through the eCFR versioner API (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-08-31/title-15.xml?part=740 and ...?part=742). The canonical eCFR HTML section URLs are cited alongside; they returned a bot-block redirect from this network, not a 404.

headline: The US moved H200-class chips for China and Macau from presumed denial to case-by-case review, subject to a 50% cap and third-party testing.
notes: Final rule, Federal Register citation 91 FR 1684, document 2026-00789, published and effective 2026-01-15; announced by BIS 2026-01-13. UNIT IS A PERCENTAGE CAP, not a volume. Covers the Nvidia H200 and equivalents (BIS names the AMD MI325X) and less advanced chips, provided they were commercially available in the US at publication. Exporter must certify sufficient US supply, that production for China will not divert foundry capacity from US end users, that the recipient has adequate security and export compliance procedures including customer screening, and that the item has passed independent third-party testing in the United States. Follows the President's 2025-12-08 announcement. RELEVANCE TO APAC MATCHING: it loosens China only; it does not change the worldwide licence requirement that governs sales into India or Southeast Asia.
quantity_raw: aggregate shipments to China and Macau not more than 50% of the total quantity shipped to US customers for domestic use

headline: The US moved the UAE into its closest export-control tier and named G42 and Core42 as able to receive AI chips without a licence.
notes: Final rule, Federal Register citation 91 FR 43034, document 2026-14132, published 2026-07-14, effective 2026-07-10. BIS removed the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and added it to A:5, and made License Exception STA available. Consistent with the May 2025 US-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, the UAE Government and approved commercial entities get licence-free access to advanced computing items. Supplement No. 8 to Part 740 names the approved UAE consignees: Group 42 Holding Ltd d/b/a G42 including G42 Cloud Technology LLC, and Core42 Technology Projects LLC - both authorised for 'Advanced Computing Items Consistent with 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)-(B)' at 91 FR 43038, 7/10/2026. The same supplement lists US firms authorised for the UAE: Amazon.com, Apple, Google, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, OpenAI Group PBC, Oracle and X.AI. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR ASIA: the UAE now has a licence-free lane that India, Singapore and Southeast Asia do not, so it competes for the same supply on better terms. The UAE reaffirmed a commitment to matching investments in US AI infrastructure.

headline: Any company at least 50% owned by an Entity-Listed or Military End User-Listed firm is now automatically restricted too.
notes: Interim final rule published in the Federal Register 2025-09-30, document 2025-19001, 'Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities'. Restrictions immediately effective with some exceptions up to 60 days after publication. Significant minority ownership by a listed company is a red flag triggering additional due diligence. Licence review policy for listed parties is generally a presumption of denial. UNIT IS AN OWNERSHIP PERCENTAGE. WHY IT MATTERS IN APAC: many Southeast Asian and Indian colocation and cloud counterparties have opaque or minority Chinese shareholdings; this rule converts an ownership fact into an automatic licence requirement, so counterparty screening now has to run the cap table, not just the name.
quantity_raw: at least 50 percent owned by one or more entities on the Entity List or the MEU List

headline: Applied Materials paid a $252m penalty for shipping controlled equipment through its Korean arm to an Entity-Listed Chinese customer.
notes: Settlement with Applied Materials Inc. and Applied Materials Korea, Ltd. The second-highest penalty ever imposed by BIS, and twice the transaction value, the statutory maximum. In 2021 and 2022 AMAT shipped ion implanters to AMK in Korea for assembly and then onward to China without a licence, after the Chinese customer was placed on the Entity List in 2020. AMAT also agreed to repeated export compliance audits and annual certifications, and the responsible compliance and executive staff left the company. THE APAC LESSON: transiting through an A:5 ally does not launder a shipment; the enforcement risk attaches to the final destination. Investigated by BIS Office of Export Enforcement Boston Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations.
quantity_raw: penalty of approximately $252 million; value of merchandise illegally shipped approximately $126 million
